\section{New interventions, mechanism proposals and information value}

Lampinen and colleagues show how passive learning from expert demonstrations
can support active causal strategies \cite{v12_la_2305_16183}. Their
constructive argument first acquires causal information through experiments,
then exploits it. The evaluated learner can intervene in its test environment.
This is a valuable qualification: passive training is co

ositive finding concerns learning
how to investigate from examples of competent investigation. At evaluation,
the learner can act and obtain the consequences needed by the task. Passive
training is therefore compatible with active information acquisition; it is
not evidence that an observationally unidentified effect becomes identified
without new assumptions or observations. The paper's finite graphs and
constrained action and observation spaces also limit transfer to a bank with
latent customer states, delayed outcomes and restricted actions
\cite{v12_la_2305_16183}.

This distinction suggests a useful proposal component. Demonstration traces
can teach an agent to ask for the outcome horizon, request a missing
assignment variable, or select a discriminating synthetic intervention.

\section{Retrieval, constraints and soft priors}

Retrieval changes the information available to a model. It may supply an
operational definition or an expert restriction that the numerical data cannot
identify. It can also supply irrelevant or contradictory evidence. Zhang and
colleagues' retrieval-assisted method reports mixed results: in the inspected
ASIA setting, documents reduce skeleton F1 from 1 to 0.73, while other settings
benefit \cite{v12_la_2402_15301}. The result argues for keeping retrieval
conditions visible in a comparison, rather than labeling retrieval as a
uniform improvement.

The reported orientation accuracy in that work is evaluated on recovered
true-positi

t specification, not a theorem that every target is identified. Its
purpose is to make semantic changes observable.

The literature supplies several useful components but no generally qualified
substitute for this contract. Causal discovery assistants can separate user
decisions from formal algorithm outputs; retrieval systems can attach passages;
benchmark environments can require structured identification and estimation
